title: Dashboards: Making Charts and Graphs Easier to Understand (NN/g)
reliability_notes: Nielsen Norman Group is a leading, evidence-based UX research organization; article is grounded in preattentive-processing perception research, not trend opinion. Primary/authoritative.
key_claims_supported: Dashboards defined as single-page, at-a-glance data-visualization collections for fast action
Operational vs analytical dashboard distinction
Preattentive processing favors length and 2D position for quantitative data
Bar/line/scatter charts outperform pie charts, gauges, and 3D charts for dashboards
Color should encode category, not quantity/magnitude; ~8% of men have color-vision deficiency

title: Progressive Disclosure (NN/g)
reliability_notes: Primary NN/g research article; foundational IA/interaction-design concept with cited usability rationale (learnability, efficiency, error reduction).
key_claims_supported: Progressive disclosure shows essential options first, defers advanced/rare features to secondary screens
Improves learnability, efficiency, and error prevention
Requires correct primary/secondary feature split and clear disclosure mechanics
More than two disclosure levels tends to hurt usability

title: F-Shaped Pattern of Reading on the Web: Misunderstood, But Still Relevant (NN/g)
reliability_notes: NN/g eye-tracking research; original and updated findings on scanning behavior. Primary/authoritative.
key_claims_supported: Users scan in F/Z-shaped patterns: horizontal sweep top, shorter second sweep, vertical scan down the left
Most important content/metrics belong in the top-left / upper area

title: 10 Usability Heuristics for User Interface Design (NN/g, Jakob Nielsen)
reliability_notes: The canonical, most widely cited usability heuristics checklist in the UX field (1994, still primary reference). Authoritative.
key_claims_supported: Visibility of system status, match with real world, user control/freedom, consistency/standards
Error prevention, recognition over recall, flexibility/efficiency, aesthetic/minimalist design
Help users recover from errors, help/documentation
Basis for catching dashboard anti-patterns via heuristic evaluation

title: Microinteractions in User Experience (NN/g)
reliability_notes: Primary NN/g article on microinteractions, aligned with Dan Saffer's foundational framework.
key_claims_supported: Microinteractions are small, single-purpose product moments (trigger, rules, feedback, loops/modes)
Used for hover/focus/click feedback and status changes

title: Response Time Limits: Article by Jakob Nielsen (NN/g)
reliability_notes: Classic, widely cited NN/g research on the 0.1s/1s/10s response-time thresholds for perceived responsiveness. Primary/authoritative.
key_claims_supported: 0.1s feels instantaneous, 1s keeps flow of thought, 10s is the attention limit before users disengage
Feedback for hover/click interactions should appear within ~0.1s

title: Timing Guidelines for Exposing Hidden Content (NN/g)
reliability_notes: Primary NN/g guidance on hover-triggered content timing.
key_claims_supported: Hover delay of 0.3-0.5s before showing hidden content, then reveal within 0.1s
Weak/absent hover signifiers create user uncertainty over time

title: Proximity Principle in Visual Design (NN/g)
reliability_notes: Primary NN/g article on Gestalt proximity as applied to UI grouping/hierarchy.
key_claims_supported: Elements placed close together are perceived as related/grouped
Proximity underlies card-based grouping and widget layout in dashboards

title: What are the Gestalt Principles? (Interaction Design Foundation)
reliability_notes: Interaction Design Foundation is a recognized UX education body; article surveys proximity, similarity, closure, common region, figure-ground with academic grounding in Gestalt psychology.
key_claims_supported: Gestalt principles (proximity, similarity, closure, common region, figure-ground) govern perceptual grouping in interfaces
Applied to reduce cognitive load and clarify widget/card relationships

title: The Role of Micro-interactions in Modern UX (Interaction Design Foundation)
reliability_notes: IxDF educational body; corroborates NN/g and Dan Saffer's microinteraction framework.
key_claims_supported: Microinteractions build usability, trust, and polish through small feedback moments

url_or_ref: Dan Saffer, "Microinteractions: Designing with Details" (2013) — referenced via secondary summaries (Goodreads, IxDA Seattle, Medium/Andrew Clark review)
title: Microinteractions: Designing with Details
reliability_notes: Foundational, widely cited UX book establishing the trigger/rules/feedback/loops-and-modes framework for microinteractions. Accessed via secondary summaries, not full text, but the framework is independently corroborated by NN/g's own microinteractions article.
key_claims_supported: Every microinteraction has four parts: trigger, rules, feedback, loops and modes

title: WebAIM: Contrast and Color Accessibility
reliability_notes: WebAIM is a leading, widely cited accessibility organization; article closely tracks the official WCAG 2 spec. Primary/authoritative.
key_claims_supported: WCAG AA: 4.5:1 contrast for normal text, 3:1 for large text (18pt+/14pt+bold)
WCAG AAA: 7:1 normal text, 4.5:1 large text
1.4.11 Non-text Contrast: 3:1 for UI components/graphical objects in all states (hover/focus/active)
Contrast ratios cannot be rounded up to pass

title: How screen readers navigate data tables (Tink, Léonie Watson)
reliability_notes: Author is a recognized accessibility expert and former W3C WAI-ARIA working-group co-chair; primary practitioner authority on screen-reader behavior.
key_claims_supported: Proper table markup (scope attributes, captions) enables screen-reader table navigation
Keyboard users need arrow-key navigation between cells/rows/columns (ARIA grid pattern)

title: Accessibility in amCharts 5
reliability_notes: Vendor documentation from a widely used charting library; describes concrete ARIA implementation for interactive charts. Corroborates Tink and W3C WAI-ARIA Graphics Module guidance.
key_claims_supported: Interactive charts need full keyboard operability (tab order, filters, tooltips)
Every chart should have an accessible tabular-data equivalent
aria-label/aria-describedby and live regions announce data values and updates

title: Carbon Design System — Data Visualization: Chart Anatomy / Chart Types (IBM)
reliability_notes: Official design-system documentation from IBM's Carbon Design System, a major production design system. Primary source.
key_claims_supported: Chart selection should start from the visualization's purpose
Guidance per chart family: bar (comparison), line/area (trends), stacked (proportional contribution), scatter (correlation), circular (part-to-whole)
Titles should be descriptive/qualitative and reflect the main insight

title: Material Design's Color Palette / Designing a dark theme with Material and Figma (Google Design)
reliability_notes: Official Google Material Design documentation and codelab. Primary source for a major, widely adopted design system.
key_claims_supported: Dark theme should use dark gray (#121212), not true black, as the base surface
Elevation communicated via lighter overlay tints on raised surfaces rather than shadows
Less saturated, more luminous accent tones (recommend desaturating toward tone ~200) on dark surfaces
Recommends higher (15.8:1) text/background contrast in dark theme vs. AA minimum

title: 10 Best Practices for Dark Mode UI Design
reliability_notes: Design-practice blog; not a primary standard, but content aligns closely with Material Design's official dark-theme guidance and WCAG contrast rules, providing independent corroboration.
key_claims_supported: Avoid pure black backgrounds and pure white text (use off-white/light gray)
Surface hierarchy via progressively lighter layered surfaces (e.g. #0B0E13 base, #11151C card, #171C24 hover)
Use semi-bold/medium type weights on dark backgrounds; avoid thin fonts and italics
Secondary text/placeholder/disabled elements are the most common contrast failures in dark mode
Use tabular figures for aligned numeric columns

title: Dashboard Design UX Patterns Best Practices (Pencil & Paper)
reliability_notes: Credible design-practice publication with detailed, reasoned pattern analysis (not a listicle); widely referenced in the dashboard-design UX community.
key_claims_supported: Curate dashboard content deliberately; 'we have it so why show it' is an anti-pattern
Top-down hierarchy: global numbers/most relevant data top-left, following F/Z scan patterns
Consistent card layout (title/legend/accessory placement) reduces visual noise
Avoid literal stoplight red-yellow-green; use intensity gradients; pair color with texture/pattern for colorblind users
Always show deltas/baselines for comparative context
Progressive disclosure via tooltips/hover; both global and module-level filters

title: Interaction Patterns UX Design Guide (Pencil & Paper)
reliability_notes: Same credible design-practice publication as above; corroborates NN/g and IxDF on microinteractions/affordance.
key_claims_supported: Affordances (raised buttons, text-field cursors, slider thumbs) signal how elements can be used
Hover/focus states provide visual guidance especially in complex interfaces

title: Empty State UX Examples & Best Practices (Pencil & Paper)
reliability_notes: Credible design-practice publication; content corroborated by Toptal and UXPin empty-state guidance.
key_claims_supported: Empty states should explain why the state is empty and provide a clear call-to-action
Avoid generic placeholder copy ('no data'); use positive, non-blaming language

title: Dashboard Design: Best Practices With Examples (Toptal)
reliability_notes: Toptal's design publication is a reasoned, evidence-referencing practitioner source (cites data-ink ratio, progressive disclosure) rather than a trend listicle.
key_claims_supported: Effective dashboards are clear, fast, customizable, and prioritize data with drill-down
Progressive disclosure reduces error rates and improves efficiency
Data-ink ratio: minimize non-data pixels, use separate cards over screen-filling graphs
Dark themes suit extended-use B2B SaaS dashboards to reduce eye strain, with trade-offs

title: Six Principles of Dashboard Information Architecture (GoodData)
reliability_notes: Vendor blog (GoodData is an analytics platform) — moderate reliability; used only as corroboration alongside NN/g and Pencil & Paper, not as a standalone claim source.
key_claims_supported: Structure, navigation, hierarchy, grouping, labeling, and filtering as core dashboard IA principles

title: Spacing, grids, and layouts (designsystems.com)
reliability_notes: Aggregator/reference site surveying spacing conventions across major production design systems (Material, iOS HIG, Carbon, Fluent); moderate-to-good reliability as a cross-system corroborating source.
key_claims_supported: 8pt spacing grid (8/16/24/32/40/48px multiples), with 4px half-step, adopted across most major design systems
4pt baseline grid pairs with 8pt UI grid for predictable typographic scaling

title: Web Design Trends 2026: What Actually Held Up After Six Months (Studio Meyer)
reliability_notes: Practitioner retrospective with concrete performance data (FPS drops, scroll-depth stats, adoption percentages) rather than a forward-looking trend roundup; more evidence-grounded than typical trend-listicle content, but represents a single agency's account.
key_claims_supported: Bento grid layouts and dark mode proved durable/usability-grounded, now standard in major products
Glassmorphism 2.0 survives only in limited contexts (nav/modals) due to real performance cost (15-30% FPS drop from backdrop-filter blur)
Kinetic typography and heavy 3D/WebGL largely failed to deliver in production due to accessibility and performance costs
Token-based design systems, not superficial CSS trends, are what modern dark-mode implementations actually require

title: Bento Grid Dashboard Design: Complete Guide 2026 (Orbix Studio)
reliability_notes: Design-agency blog, SEO-content flavored — lower reliability, used only as volume corroboration for the bento-grid trend description, not as sole support for any claim.
key_claims_supported: Bento grids use modular mixed-size blocks (large feature + small supporting) for dashboards/overview pages, improving scanability

title: Crafting A Killer Brand Identity For A Digital Product (Smashing Magazine)
reliability_notes: Smashing Magazine is a long-established, reputable web-design publication with editorial review, stronger than typical listicle content.
key_claims_supported: Differentiation in visually saturated markets comes from subtlety, restraint, and organic/human-scale design choices rather than louder aesthetics

title: Why some designs look messy, and others don't (UX Collective / Prototypr)
reliability_notes: UX Collective is a large, editorially curated design-practice publication; moderate-to-good reliability, corroborates Smashing Magazine's differentiation argument from a different angle (visual order vs brand voice).
key_claims_supported: Templated/mass-market design standardizes structure irrespective of content needs, producing genericness
A tight connection between content and form (rather than templated separation) is what produces distinctive, non-generic design

title: Dashboard Anti-Patterns: 12 Mistakes—and the Patterns That Replace Them
reliability_notes: Independent design-practice article enumerating specific, falsifiable anti-patterns rather than generic trend advice; moderate reliability, corroborated by NN/g heuristics and Pencil & Paper on several specific points (context/hierarchy/chart-type mistakes).
key_claims_supported: Common anti-patterns: metric overload, vanity-metric prominence, missing context, poor hierarchy, wrong chart types, excessive interactivity, unclear objectives
Working-memory limit (~5-9 elements) argues for capping metrics per screen
Truncated/non-zero Y-axes mislead viewers about magnitude of change

title: Navigating Data Visualization: A Guide to Chart Junk Awareness (The Data School)
reliability_notes: Secondary explainer of Edward Tufte's original chartjunk/data-ink-ratio concept; The Data School is a data-visualization training organization. Corroborated independently by Toptal and NN/g's own chart-type guidance.
key_claims_supported: Chartjunk (Tufte's term) refers to decorative elements (3D effects, shadows, excess gridlines) that reduce clarity
Data-to-ink ratio: most pixels should represent data, not decoration

title: How to Use Skeleton Screens to Improve Perceived Website Performance (freeCodeCamp)
reliability_notes: freeCodeCamp is a well-established developer-education nonprofit publication; moderate-to-good reliability, corroborated by multiple independent design blogs on the same mechanism (perceived vs actual performance).
key_claims_supported: Skeleton screens mimic final layout with placeholders, improving perceived load speed without changing actual load time
Preferred over spinners for content-heavy interfaces like dashboards and feeds because they convey structural progress
